item.title: hoop2vec prospects: the draft and what comes after
item.description:
I’ve always thought the eye test was worth something. Not just for seeing a player’s skills, but for seeing how competitive they are and what their drive is like. I knew Marcus Smart and Christian Braun were going to play hard at the next level. I could tell Trae Young was going to be a difficult talent to fit around, and that Andrew Wiggins didn’t have the killer instinct you’d want. But for the most part, who gets drafted and who sticks in the pros can be modeled with reasonable accuracy.

The college sites on hoop2vec have a Prospects page that runs two of those models on every player: NBA prospects on the men’s site and WNBA prospects on the women’s.

Two models

The draft model estimates the chance a player is picked in each tier of the draft, from the very top down to getting picked at all. For the NBA that’s the top 5, the lottery (the top 14), the first round, and both rounds. The WNBA draft is three rounds and 36 picks, so its tiers are the top 4, the top 12, the top 24, and drafted. The model learned from every past college player-season and who actually got drafted.

The success model estimates the chance a player becomes a real contributor early in a pro career, measured in Win Shares, a stat that splits a team’s wins among its players. In the NBA the bar is 8 Win Shares in the first four seasons, about what a steady rotation player gets. WNBA seasons are shorter and the rosters are smaller, so the bar there is 2.5 Win Shares in the first three seasons. Players who went undrafted or never made it are in the data too, as misses.

Both models use age, height, class, team and conference strength, role, and a few dozen stats adjusted for opponents. On the men’s side, age matters more than anything else. A freshman putting up good numbers at 18 is a much better bet than a senior putting up the same numbers at 23. There aren’t free birth dates or recruiting rankings for women’s players, so class and height have to stand in.

How well it works

I tested the models one draft at a time, training each only on earlier drafts. In the NBA version, an average of 20 of the model’s top 30 players were drafted, compared with about 15 for a simple baseline using recruiting ranking, box plus/minus, and age. The WNBA version is about as good at picking who gets drafted, and better than its baseline at predicting the order.

Pro teams are still better at this than I am, in both leagues. For players who were drafted, where they were picked predicts their careers better than my success model does. Teams get workouts, medical reports, and interviews. I get box scores. The models also only cover college players, so international and G League prospects aren’t on the board, and the board’s slots run ahead of where players will really go.

Each prospect also gets comps. A separate model learns how college stats turn into pro stats over a player’s first few seasons, then finds past college players at the same stage whose projected pro profile is closest, and shows what they became. Some things carry over better than others. On the men’s side, rebounding, blocks, assists, and how many threes a player takes translate well. Shooting efficiency and overall impact translate much less.

ESPN, KenPom, or Sports Reference could show this kind of detail in a way that’s easy to use. They have years of existing pages to work around, and I got to start from scratch.

item.title: The hoop2vec model that was too good
item.description:
Everyone who works with data leaks it eventually. Leakage is when a model gets to see information it wouldn’t have had at the moment it’s supposed to be predicting, and it’s very easy to do by accident. When you test a basketball model on past seasons, you pretend it’s the morning of each game. The hard part is making sure the model only knows what someone could have known that morning. If anything from later sneaks in, the model looks better than it really is.

An early version of hoop2vec had a leak. In testing, it beat the betting lines on men’s NCAA tournament games, which a model built on free public data shouldn’t be able to do. Sportsbooks have the same data and a lot more reason to get it right. So I went looking for the problem.

The leak was in a player stat that rates every player for every game, an estimate of how much each one helped their team that night. To make those ratings fair, the stat adjusts for how good the team and the opponent are, and it does that using each team’s rating from the end of the season. That’s fine for looking back on a season, which is what the stat is meant for. It’s a problem for predicting one. Add up a team’s player ratings in November and you get a number that partly knows how good the team will be in March.

On its own, that one number beat the betting line in all ten seasons I checked. Once I redid the player ratings using only the team ratings from the morning of each game, the same number lost to the line in all ten. The full model got worse too. Its tournament forecasts went from beating the betting lines to trailing them slightly, which is about where an honest public-data model should be.

The same symptom came up again when I added women’s college basketball. The women’s model slightly beats the few sportsbook lines ESPN carries for those games. Women’s betting markets are thinner, so that’s plausible, but it’s exactly what the men’s leak looked like. So I ran the same check. The player ratings alone did worse than the line, and the plain dynamic rating was about even with it. The edge there is more likely a thin market than a leak.

If you’re newer to data science, you’ll leak data at some point too. Take steps to avoid it, check for it when results look too good, and be honest about it when it happens.

item.title: hoop2vec predictions: every game, every morning
item.description:
Every game in all four leagues on hoop2vec gets a forecast: a predicted score, a margin, and a win probability. They’re on each league’s Games page and on every team’s page, and they update every morning with the latest results and injury news.

The Matchup Lab lets you set up any game yourself. You pick two teams and a site, and the full model runs in your browser. It shows the forecast and how much each piece mattered: team strength, home court, travel, rest, injuries, and matchup effects. Moving a close college game from one team’s gym to a neutral floor can turn a clear favorite into something close to a coin flip.

How it works

The forecast blends two models. One is a neural network that takes about 40 numbers for each team, from both ratings to shooting, rebounding, turnovers, roster strength, injuries, rest, and travel. It sees both teams at once, so it can pick up on styles that match up well or badly. The other is a plain linear model built on team ratings, home court, travel, rest, and injuries. It can’t learn matchups, but it’s harder to fool.

How much weight each model gets depends on the league, and the backtest picks it. In men’s college basketball and the NBA, the network gets 70 percent. In the women’s college game it gets 80. The WNBA only has 15 teams and a short season, so there isn’t much data, and the backtest leans the other way and gives the linear model 70 percent.

The model also estimates how uncertain each game is. Some matchups are harder to call than others, and the forecast says how far the final margin is likely to land from the prediction.

To test it, I had each league’s model predict every past game as if it were the morning of the game. It could only learn from earlier seasons, and it only saw injury news that was public before tip-off. For men’s college basketball that’s about 82,000 games since 2012, and the model picked the winner in 73.5 percent of them. The score I care more about is log loss, which punishes a confident wrong forecast much harder than an unsure one. In men’s and women’s college basketball and the NBA, the blend beat each of its parts and every rating it’s built from. The WNBA’s history is short enough that all the models land within noise of each other.

Against the books

The toughest comparison is a sportsbook. ESPN carries closing betting lines for some games, set right before tip-off, and they’re more accurate than the model in men’s college basketball and the NBA. The gap is bigger in the NBA, where the betting market is sharper. In women’s college basketball the model slightly beats the few lines ESPN carries, which made me suspicious enough to check it for leaks. More on that in its own post.

Around 2020 I was burned out from open-source work and the never-ending demands of teaching, research, and mentoring. So naturally I spent my free time trying to beat the stock market, predict elections, and model sports betting. What I found is that models are useful, but an actual edge comes from data other people don’t have, or from knowing something they don’t. A model built on public data usually ends up close to the betting line and a little behind it.

What I want from hoop2vec is information that’s easy to read and as accurate as I can make it. It helps me figure out who’s actually good, who’s overrated, which teams are worth following, and which ones would be fun to pencil in on a bracket.
